title: Styling a Quarto Website with CSS & SCSS
text:
Quarto handles the structure of a website, like pages, the navbar, and the table of contents. CSS controls how it looks, like colors, fonts, spacing, and borders. SCSS is CSS with extra features, and the most useful one is variables. You define a color once and reuse it everywhere, so changing one line updates the whole site.






TipWhy this matters for a portfolio



A built-in theme makes a site look clean, but every Quarto site using it looks the same. A small SCSS file is the easiest way to make a portfolio feel personal and on brand.

title: Styling a Quarto Website with CSS & SCSS
section: How Quarto Uses an SCSS File
text:
How Quarto Uses an SCSS File
There are three steps.

Start with a built-in Bootstrap theme. This site uses cosmo.
Write a .scss file with your own variables and rules.
Tell _quarto.yml to layer your file on top of the theme.



_quarto.yml

format:
  html:
    theme: [cosmo, custom.scss]

The square brackets mean “start with cosmo, then apply my file on top.”

title: Styling a Quarto Website with CSS & SCSS
section: The Two Sections of an SCSS File
text:
The Two Sections of an SCSS File
Quarto needs two labeled sections so it knows when to apply each part.








Section
What goes in it
When it applies




/*-- scss:defaults --*/
Variables like colors and fonts
Before the theme is built


/*-- scss:rules --*/
Regular CSS rules
After the theme is built

What Changed on This Site

NavbarFontsDetailsDashboard


The navbar uses blush instead of the default cosmo color, set with $navbar-bg.


Headings use Playfair Display and body text uses Nunito, set with $headings-font-family and $font-family-sans-serif.


Every h2 has a blush underline, images have rounded corners, and bold text is dusty rose. You can see the bold rule on my Home page skill labels.


My CEP dashboard reuses the same custom.scss, so it matches the rest of the site.

title: Styling a Quarto Website with CSS & SCSS
text:
What I Learned
The biggest takeaway for me was how much a few variables can change. Once the palette was defined, I didn’t have to style each page separately. If I want to rebrand later, I only need to swap the hex codes in one file.

title: Using Listings to Build a Portfolio
text:
A listing is a Quarto feature that automatically builds a page of links from other pages in your project. Instead of writing a link for every project by hand, you point the listing at a folder, and Quarto reads each file’s title, description, and categories to build the cards.






TipWhy it’s useful for a portfolio



When I add a new project, I just drop a new .qmd file into the projects folder. The listing updates itself the next time the site renders.

text:
A listing is a Quarto feature that automatically builds a page of links from other pages in your project. Instead of writing a link for every project by hand, you point the listing at a folder, and Quarto reads each file’s title, description, and categories to build the cards.






TipWhy it’s useful for a portfolio

title: Using Listings to Build a Portfolio
text:
How It Works
The listing is set up in this page’s YAML header:


listings.qmd

listing:
  contents: projects      # folder to pull pages from
  type: grid              # card layout (other options: default, table)
  categories: true        # adds clickable category filters
  sort: "title"
  fields: [title, description, categories]
  grid-columns: 3

Each project page only needs a short header:


projects/efcu-dashboard.qmd

---
title: "EFCU Member Opinion Dashboard"
description: "A Quarto dashboard summarizing a credit union member survey."
categories: [Dashboard, R, Survey Research]
---

title: My Culminating Experience Project
text:
For my MSDM Culminating Experience Project, my team is working with Wellness Ranch Equine Assisted Therapy, a nonprofit that offers equine assisted therapy. Our project focuses on implementing and optimizing the ranch’s digital marketing, including website and SEO improvements, GA4 analytics, and Google Ad Grants preparation. My part of the project is the SEO performance analysis.
Because our GA4 tracking is still collecting data, I built this first dashboard with the Case 31 practice dataset. It lets me work out the layout and charts now, so I can swap in the ranch’s data once there is enough of it.

title: My Culminating Experience Project
text:
What the Dashboard Answers
The credit union’s board wanted to understand why members were not borrowing money from the credit union. The dashboard is organized around the questions they needed answered:

How do members feel about credit union employees?
How aware are members of the services offered?
How do members feel about borrowing from the credit union?
Do members who live near headquarters feel differently from members who live elsewhere?

title: My Culminating Experience Project
text:
How I Built It
The dashboard is a separate Quarto file that uses format: dashboard instead of format: html. In a dashboard, headings control the layout rather than the text:

A level one heading (#) creates a new page in the dashboard.
A level two heading (## Row) creates a row, and each code chunk inside it becomes a card.
A chunk with #| content: valuebox turns a single number into a highlighted value box.

Here is the code behind one of the value boxes:


cep-dashboard.qmd

#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Currently have an EFCU loan"
pct_loan <- mean(efcu$q27 == 1) * 100
list(icon = "cash-coin", color = blush, value = paste0(round(pct_loan), "%"))

The charts are made with ggplot2 and use the same pink neutral palette as the rest of this site, so the dashboard feels like part of the portfolio.
